name: Carlos Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the rebuild crew for the dry south of the district, so a lot of my work is after fires. A wildfire goes through, burns forty poles, and we go in and put the line back up, sometimes through ash up to your ankles. In the quiet months it's hardening work, swapping wooden poles for steel ones and putting in switches that cut the power automatically if a line comes down, so it doesn't start a fire.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the rebuilds, honestly. There's nothing like driving out of a black valley with the line humming again. What wears me out is the heat, and being paid like a junior when I'm doing the same work as men with twenty years. I live with my younger brother, I help with his college fees, and last year I put most of my savings into a used drone and the licence to fly it, so right now I've got maybe two weeks of money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Because I can see where this is going. I use AI every day, to plan routes, to read the fire maps, to study. I fly the drone over burned sections on my days off to practise spotting damaged poles. One day I want my own small line contracting company, and drones are going to be part of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still good, people just expected miracles. I'd keep telling the guys at the yard to use them, because they save time. Online I'd post a few drone clips, nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a little disappointed. I'd bet on things moving faster, and that's what my drone is for. But it's fine, the rebuild work is steady, and fires aren't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Keep using AI to study for my next grade. Fly the drone for a few farmers on weekends, checking fences and irrigation, maybe eighty a visit, to rebuild the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your brother's college fees. How much do they weigh on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a quarter of what I have left each month. Our father had a stroke two years ago, so it's on me now. I'd rather be broke with my brother in college than comfortable with him stacking shelves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your crewmates, do they use the tools you use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some do now. The old foreman, Ramón, used to laugh. Now he asks me to check the fire map on my phone before we drive in. That's how it works: you prove it, then they come.

S0.say: The tools are still good, people just expected miracles. He'd keep telling the crew to use them and post a few drone clips online.
S0.think: He'd be a little disappointed, having bet on faster change with his drone, but rebuild work after fires stays steady.
S0.do: Keeps working and uses AI to study for his next grade. Flies his drone for local farmers on weekends, at about eighty a visit, to rebuild his savings.
S0.quote: I'd rather be broke with my brother in college than comfortable with him stacking shelves.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos has already bet his savings on a drone, so he's ahead of the change rather than afraid of it. His thin cushion comes from supporting his brother after his father's stroke. He believes people adopt new tools once they're proven, like his foreman did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for anyone willing to work and learn. The ones who move early win, the ones who wait complain. I'd say it at the yard, maybe a bit more politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's my chance. The company is going to need inspection drones and people who understand both poles and software. I'd want to start my own small contract outfit doing fire-damage surveys for the company and the farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd register a small business in the first few months and start offering drone surveys after fires. I'd keep my line job while it's still worth having. I'd put the first earnings into a better drone with a thermal camera, about three thousand, paid in instalments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, really. It's what I've been waiting for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three thousand in instalments with two weeks' savings. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it is. But I'd only buy it once I had two or three paying clients. Every man in my family who got ahead did it by borrowing a little and working like a mule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ramón, actually. He came round on the phone, but he's fifty-nine. If the crews get smaller, he's the one they'll push to retire early. I'd offer him work with me if he wanted it, reading the drone pictures. He knows a burned pole better than any camera.

S1.say: This is good news for anyone willing to work and learn: those who move early win and those who wait complain. He'd say it at the yard, a bit more politely.
S1.think: It's his chance, because the company will need drone inspection and people who know both poles and software. He wants his own small contracting outfit doing fire-damage surveys.
S1.do: Registers a small business within months, offers drone surveys after fires and keeps his line job meanwhile. Buys a thermal-camera drone for about three thousand in instalments once he has two or three paying clients.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, as if this is what he's been waiting for.
S1.quote: Every man in my family who got ahead did it by borrowing a little and working like a mule.
S1.fieldNote: He sees Steady Disruption as an opening and plans to start a business, not just learn a tool. His family story of borrowing and hard work shapes his risk-taking. He'd offer his older foreman a place, valuing his eye over the camera.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This is AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say things are moving, and people need to move with them instead of waiting for the government to save them. Families have to stick together. I'd say that at the yard and to my brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's scary even for me. If AGI can do almost any work, then it can fly my drone and read my pictures too. My plan was to be the man with the machines, but with two weeks of money I can't buy machines fast enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in, fast. Quit the line job within the year, borrow from my uncle, and try to run a small crew of robots and drones on contract for the fire rebuilds, before the big companies take it all. I'd cut everything else, and my brother would have to take a part-time job alongside college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My heart would be racing, half fear and half excitement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Asking your uncle for money. How would that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say yes and then remind me at every family dinner for ten years. I'd rather owe my uncle and own a robot than be owed nothing by a company that let me go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the big companies might take it all. What makes you think a small crew could compete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it can't. I don't know. But in the first year, the big companies are slow and the fires don't wait. If I could get two or three contracts in the south, I'd have something before they arrived.

S2.say: Things are moving and people need to move with them instead of waiting for the government to save them. Families have to stick together.
S2.think: It's scary even for him: AGI could fly his drone and read his images, and with two weeks of money he can't buy machines fast enough to be the owner.
S2.do: Quits the line job within the year, borrows from his uncle and tries to run a small robot and drone crew on fire-rebuild contracts before big companies move in. Cuts all other spending, and his brother takes a part-time job alongside college.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a racing heart that's half fear and half excitement.
S2.quote: I'd rather owe my uncle and own a robot than be owed nothing by a company that let me go.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most forward-leaning person in this job finds the fast timeline frightening, because he lacks the capital to own the machines. His answer is to borrow from family, not seek state help. He's frank that a small crew may not compete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now AGI by 2031. The same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone with a bit of drive. Learn the tools, save, start something. I'd tell the younger guys at the yard that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is about right for me. Enough to build the drone business up while I still have my salary, and to get a couple of robots once they're cheaper. I'd be one of the owners when it arrives, at least a small one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Register the business in year one, do surveys on weekends, and put every spare cent back in. Save a bit, maybe a hundred a month, so I'm not living on the edge. Get my brother through his last year of college before I take a big risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fired up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm gambling with borrowed money. Five years, I'm building with my own. With five years I don't have to bet the house, I can build it brick by brick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still keep the line job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first three years, yes. It pays the bills and keeps me in the trade. I'd only leave when the business was paying more than the job, not before.

S3.say: Five years is plenty for anyone with drive: learn the tools, save and start something. He'd tell the younger crew that.
S3.think: Five years suits him, letting him grow the drone business on his salary and buy robots once they're cheaper, so he'd be a small owner when AGI arrives.
S3.do: Registers the business in year one, runs weekend surveys and reinvests every spare cent while saving about a hundred a month. Keeps the line job for three years and sees his brother through college before taking a big risk.
S3.quote: With five years I don't have to bet the house, I can build it brick by brick.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lets him grow from his own money instead of borrowing. He's more cautious here than in the fast scenario, keeping his salary until the business beats it. Getting his brother through college comes before any big risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for people who are willing to work. Get a trade, get skills, start something. No one should sit around waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be thirty-seven, and I'd hope to have a small company with a few robots, a few drones and a couple of good people. I'm not scared of that future, I want a piece of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a short business course in the first year, nights, to learn the money side properly, because I can fly a drone but I can't do accounts. Build the survey business slowly while keeping the line job. Start buying robots for line inspection and minor repairs once the prices come down, around year five or six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Confident, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change any personal plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably I'd wait to marry until the business was steady. My mother wouldn't like that, she wants grandchildren. I'd tell her I'm building something for the grandchildren first, and she'd still say I'm too slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you, if anything, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the big companies swallow everything by the end. Then I'm just a small man with old robots. But that's business. You take the chance.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift for those willing to work: get a trade, get skills, start something, and don't sit around waiting.
S4.think: He'd be 37 and hopes to run a small company with a few robots, drones and good people. He's not scared of that future and wants a piece of it.
S4.do: Takes a night business course in year one to learn accounts and builds the survey business slowly while keeping the line job. Buys robots for line inspection and minor repairs once prices fall, around year five or six.
S4.quote: I'd tell her I'm building something for the grandchildren first, and she'd still say I'm too slow.
S4.fieldNote: This is where his entrepreneurial streak fits best: time to learn the money side and buy robots cheaply. He'd delay marriage to build the business first. His one worry is big companies swallowing everything, which he accepts as part of business.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to build, only to gamble. What would help is cheap loans for workers starting small businesses in their own trade, and less red tape to register one. And keep apprenticeships going, so young people still learn real skills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people like me want to fight it. Most people assume lineworkers hate this stuff. I don't want to stop the robots, I want to be the one who owns the truck they ride in.

headlineQuote: I don't want to stop the robots, I want to be the one who owns the truck they ride in.
portrait: Carlos is a 27-year-old lineworker on a rebuild crew that puts power lines back up after wildfires in the dry south. He supports his younger brother through college after their father's stroke and put most of his savings into a drone and a pilot's licence, leaving about two weeks of money. He uses AI every day and dreams of his own small contracting company. He's calm through AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, seeing the second as his chance to start a drone survey business. AGI by 2028 makes him anxious because he can't afford machines fast enough, while five or ten years let him build steadily toward owning robots himself.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time to build a business, only to gamble on borrowed money.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans and less red tape for workers starting small businesses in their own trade, and apprenticeships kept going for young people.
